title: Practical productivity: AI can save or consume time
desc: Compares real task effects, learning, verification and interaction costs, distinguishing perceived usefulness from measured gains.

kps.k: The cluster tests whether AI improves human work in practice, rather than treating model capability or adoption as proof of productivity.
kps.d: Its substantive proposition is that benefits depend on the task, worker, interface and workflow, and that speed, quality, learning and verification costs require separate measurement. Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier claims substantial but uneven benefits from spring-2023 GPT-4 experiments with BCG consultants, while stressing that capability boundaries remain difficult to anticipate. The systematic review supplies a useful comparison framework—humans alone, AI alone and their combination—but the supplied excerpts report no pooled results. Improvement over unaided humans therefore should not be confused with evidence that collaboration outperforms AI alone.

qs.q: Our results show that this generation of LLMs are highly capable of causing significant increases in quality and productivity, or even completely automating some tasks, but the actual tasks that AI can do are surprising and not immediately obvious to individuals or even to producers of LLMs themselves.
qs.a: Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier: Field Experimental Evidence of the Effects of AI on Knowledge Worker Productivity and Quality · Academia · 2023

qs.q: To calculate our primary outcome of interest – the effect of combining human and artificial intelligence on task performance – we recorded the averages and standard deviations of the task performance of the human alone, the AI alone, and the human and AI working with each other, as well as the number of subjects in each of these conditions (see S1.3 for details).
qs.a: When Combinations of Humans and AI Are Useful: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis · Academia · 2024

kps.k: Measured time effects range from substantial savings to slower completion; these findings concern different settings, not a single universal AI effect.
kps.d: Scaling Laws for Economic Productivity reports 31.1% less translation time when pooling thirteen AI models, but its 0.14-standard-deviation quality increase was not statistically significant (p=0.148). When Help Hurts reports 22% less coding time and higher unit-test correctness odds (OR 1.71). In contrast, Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity finds 19% more completion time across 246 tasks undertaken by 16 experienced repository contributors using primarily Cursor with Claude 3.5/3.7 Sonnet during February–June 2025. How AI Impacts Skill Formation finds no conclusive timing change on unfamiliar-library tasks. Task scope, quality standards, participant expertise and model vintage limit direct comparisons; the percentages describe changes in time, not equivalent changes in work rate.

kps.k: Easier assisted completion can coexist with weaker immediate learning, but the evidence does not establish inevitable long-term deskilling.
kps.d: In How AI Impacts Skill Formation, 52 programmers learning Trio scored 4.15 points lower on a 27-point unaided quiz with AI assistance (d=0.738, p=0.01). All AI participants completed the second task, whereas four controls did not, separating completion success from understanding. Exploratory analysis found the largest learning gap in debugging; the authors propose that controls learned through greater exposure to errors. Conversely, the Argentine education-gap experiment reports stronger immediate unassisted follow-up performance when AI assistance accompanies sustained engagement, without establishing a causal effect of engagement itself. The knowledge-worker critical-thinking survey reports lower perceived effort, not measured loss of ability. The concern that inhibited learning could weaken future human verification remains a conditional prediction requiring longitudinal workplace evidence.

kps.k: Verification and interaction costs can offset assistance, making interface design and selective reliance consequential.
kps.d: When Help Hurts holds GPT-4o fixed across Inline, Chat and Structured interfaces. It reports lower immediate workload but steeper fatigue accumulation with AI across repeated tasks. Its behavioral verification-load index statistically mediates about 26% of fatigue growth and 24% of stress growth; the authors treat this as consistent with a mechanism, not causal proof, and disclose that the composites were later additions. Exploratory results favor Inline for simple work, Chat for more complex work and Structured prompting for novices at medium complexity. Both very high and very low suggestion acceptance correlate with lower correctness; the estimated optimum is not a prescription to accept a fixed share. Offloading Score separately detects greater reliance under tighter time limits (p=0.018), but its model-constructed counterfactuals and annotation checks do not establish that reliance itself harms outcomes.

kps.k: Perceived usefulness, confidence and willingness to use AI do not reliably identify actual gains.
kps.d: In the early-2025 open-source trial, developers expected 24% less completion time before participation and estimated 20% less afterward, despite the measured increase; expert forecasts also overstated benefits. Trading speed for cognitive ease is one proposed explanation, not an established mechanism. Cognitive offloading and the speedup illusion reports expected savings of 68.5 seconds, but the supplied material gives no actual-time result and therefore does not independently establish an illusion. Faith in AI can narrow the futures individuals consider adds a distinct caution: apparent predictive accuracy rose across repeated box-choice rounds while the prediction policy stayed fixed, which the authors attribute to participants adapting their behavior. This is controlled behavioral evidence, not proof of workplace effects or improving model capability.

kps.k: AI can narrow performance gaps without eliminating differences in effective use; broader equalization remains contested.
kps.d: Does Generative AI Narrow Education-Based Productivity Gaps reports larger gains for lower-education participants in a self-contained business task, while higher-education participants still use the tool somewhat more effectively. Its final Argentine sample contains 1,174 participants; the supplied excerpts provide no numerical treatment-effect estimates. The 2022 GitHub Copilot experiment likewise reports greater benefits for less-experienced developers, alongside older programmers and those coding more hours daily. Neither result demonstrates expanded career entry or equalization across occupations. Generative AI and the Productivity Divide frames competing predictions that AI helps weaker workers disproportionately or rewards already advantaged users, and proposes prompting, verification, scaffolding and peer learning as mechanisms. Its supplied student-study material reports design rather than outcomes.

qs.q: Our findings indicate that AI assistance substantially raises performance for both education groups, but with larger gains among low-education participants.

kps.k: Collective creativity and teamwork require outcomes beyond individual speed or answer quality.
kps.d: How AI Ideas Affect the Creativity, Diversity, and Evolution of Human Ideas reports greater collective idea diversity under high AI exposure, using response chains and separate exposure and disclosure manipulations. That result does not establish higher individual creativity and comes from a self-selected, creativity- and technology-oriented volunteer sample. The supplied storytelling experiment describes blinded creativity assessment but provides no findings, so its title alone cannot support an opposing diversity conclusion. The Cybernetic Teammate separates individual and cross-functional team work with and without AI, while CollabSkill records human–agent interactions on occupational tasks, including law. These excerpts contribute designs, not evidence that AI replaces teammates or improves professional collaboration.

kps.k: Selection, compliance and task-order choices qualify causal estimates and become harder to manage as AI adoption spreads.
kps.d: METR's later design update reports that 30%–50% of surveyed developers withheld some tasks because they did not want to attempt them without AI, alongside recruitment difficulties among enthusiastic adopters. METR consequently regards its later estimate as a likely lower bound, but the supplied material neither quantifies the bias nor measures benefits on omitted tasks; preferences alone cannot establish those benefits. Fixed tasks improve comparability but sacrifice some realism, while developer-level assignment may reduce task selection at the cost of recruitment and statistical power. Elsewhere, attrition checks, uptake monitoring and baseline adjustment support inference without proving absence of bias. Lawyering in the Age of Artificial Intelligence explicitly acknowledges possible task-order interactions. CUPS omits an unaided baseline and therefore cannot estimate comparative productivity.

kps.k: The practical implication is to evaluate complete workflows and retained understanding locally; evidence for professional legal deployment remains limited here.
kps.d: Building a Better Lawyer reports 29.7% less completion time with highlighting-only assistance than without AI in a student experiment; it does not establish professional-practice or quality effects. Its highlighting-versus-full-AI comparison reaches only the weaker reported threshold of p<.1. Artificial Intelligence and Human Legal Reasoning separates assisted memo production from unaided comprehension, but supplies no outcome scores; AI-Powered Lawyering likewise contributes task and participation methods rather than effects. Taken together, the cluster supports testing assistance on representative work while separately tracking completion, quality, checking and rework, fatigue, and later unaided performance. Adaptive interfaces and longitudinal learning studies are author recommendations, not proven universal solutions, and the supplied evidence does not establish firm-level returns or staffing consequences.

vlens.an: The curated academia-and-research sources accept the proposition’s core and materially develop it through controlled experiments, field studies and workflow-sensitive measurement. Their common rationale is that AI productivity cannot be inferred from model capability, adoption or user sentiment: effects must be measured separately for time, quality, learning, retained understanding, appropriate reliance, verification and interaction costs, with attention to task type, worker experience, interface design and experimental validity. The empirical findings illustrate this contingency rather than a universal direction—AI reduced time in translation, highlighting-assisted legal work and one controlled coding setting, yet increased completion time for experienced open-source developers; other work found weaker immediate skill formation without a conclusive speed benefit. Further contributions distinguish perceived gains from observed performance, assisted completion from unaided follow-up performance, and final-answer correctness from appropriate reliance. Material internal variation concerns evidential completeness and setting: several excerpts provide methods only and therefore leave substantive effects unclear; reported results span students, online participants and professionals, limiting transfer across contexts; and some mechanisms, including verification-driven fatigue and long-term deskilling, remain observational, exploratory or predictive. None of the supplied sources clearly rejects the proposition, but methods-only studies should not be treated as affirmative findings. This assessment characterises only the curated sources provided, not academia or researchers generally.

vlens.an: The supplied market-analyst/consultancy/press source—METR’s design update—accepts the cluster’s principal proposition that practical productivity must be measured in real workflows rather than inferred from capability or adoption. It materially extends that proposition by showing how rising AI adoption can itself distort productivity experiments: enthusiastic adopters may decline participation, while participating developers may withhold tasks they are unwilling to perform without AI. METR therefore treats its estimate as a likely lower bound, but does not claim that omitted tasks have measured gains or quantify the resulting bias. Internal variation is methodological rather than directional: METR notes that selection affects only a minority of developers and tasks, and that proposed alternatives trade one problem for another—developer-level randomization can reduce task selection while worsening participant selection and statistical power. This evidence supports locally grounded workflow measurement while adding a concrete warning that increasingly adopted tools make representative causal measurement harder.

vlens.an: The legal-tech-vendor evidence supports the proposition that AI productivity should be established through performance on actual tasks rather than inferred from adoption or perceived usefulness, and that effects depend on worker characteristics. The randomized GitHub Copilot trial used standardized programming work and objective completion-time measures, while separately collecting participants’ estimated speed gains. It also reports heterogeneous benefits, with less-experienced, older and higher-hours programmers benefiting most. Material qualifications include the narrow standardized task, the geographically concentrated Upwork sample and incomplete treatment uptake, which limit generalization but do not undermine the proposition. Because this facet contains one curated source, it should not be treated as representative of legal-tech vendors generally.

elens.an: The 2015–2022 sources support the proposition primarily as an evaluative and methodological claim: practical productivity should be studied through observed AI-assisted work, with worker experience, training, task design and experimental constraints treated as consequential rather than assuming that access or adoption proves a gain. The TECHCO study most directly aligns with this framing by comparing the same workers under manual and algorithm-assisted conditions and treating domain experience as a moderator. Grounded Copilot is consistent with the emphasis on heterogeneous users and situated interaction, documenting prior Copilot and programming-language experience, but it lacks an unaided baseline and reports no productivity, quality, learning or verification findings in the supplied material. Thus, the period evidence supports workflow-level testing but does not itself show whether AI saved or consumed time. There is material internal variation in evidentiary strength: one source provides a comparative experimental design while acknowledging practical limitations; the other contributes only an assisted-use protocol. These curated sources should not be treated as representative of all research from the period.

elens.an: The curated 2023–2024 sources support the proposition that practical AI productivity is task-, worker-, interface- and workflow-dependent and must be established through direct measurement rather than inferred from model capability, adoption or perceived usefulness. The strongest outcome evidence reports substantial time savings in bounded tasks—31.1% in pooled-model translation and 29.7% from highlighting-only assistance in a student legal exercise—while also limiting interpretation: the translation quality gain was not statistically significant, and the legal study does not establish quality effects or professional-practice gains. The BCG experiments provide the clearest conceptual explanation for such variation, locating gains within a jagged capability frontier and showing that AI can be less reliable on deliberately outside-frontier work. The Copilot trial adds worker heterogeneity, reporting larger benefits for less-experienced, older and more intensive programmers, without demonstrating broader career equalisation. Creativity studies further show why outcomes must be separated: one reports greater collective idea diversity rather than individual productivity, while another contributes a blinded evaluation design but no supplied findings. Material internal variation is therefore mainly about what each source establishes. Some provide measured effects; several provide only experimental methods, comparison frameworks or causal qualifications; and the calibrated-judgment study supplies insufficient outcome evidence to determine a substantive productivity position. The systematic review distinguishes humans alone, AI alone and human–AI collaboration, while CUPS deliberately omits an unaided baseline and therefore cannot estimate comparative productivity. Task ordering, sample concentration, treatment non-use and unequal attrition also qualify causal and external validity. Taken together, these selected sources support local, outcome-specific workflow evaluation, but they do not establish a universal productivity effect, comprehensive verification costs, long-term learning consequences or firm-level returns.

elens.an: The selected 2025 sources collectively build on the cluster’s principal proposition that AI adoption or perceived usefulness does not itself establish practical productivity, and that effects must be measured across complete, task-specific workflows. The strongest extension is randomized evidence from experienced open-source developers showing that early-2025 AI tools increased completion time by 19% even though participants believed the tools had saved time. This materially demonstrates both a workflow-dependent cost and a divergence between perceived and measured gains. The other sources reinforce, rather than independently prove, that conclusion: the P&G field experiment separates AI assistance from human teamwork and distinguishes time, expected quality, expertise deployment and emotional outcomes, but the supplied excerpts omit its principal effect estimates; the knowledge-worker survey finds lower self-reported critical-thinking effort, but does not measure productivity or loss of ability. Internal variation is therefore mainly evidential: one source reports a negative causal time effect in a specific coding setting, one contributes a rigorous multi-outcome design without supplied results, and one documents subjective cognitive experience. None supports a universal slowdown or gain, and each leaves generalisation dependent on task, worker, interface and workflow.

elens.an: The curated 2026 sources collectively build on the proposition that practical AI productivity is workflow-dependent and must be decomposed into speed, quality, learning, reliance and verification effects. Their material contribution is a more granular measurement agenda: controlled coding evidence reports immediate reductions in time and workload alongside greater accumulated fatigue and observational verification load; a separate randomized study finds weaker immediate skill formation without a conclusive speed effect; other studies distinguish appropriate reliance from final-answer correctness, construct counterfactual workflow measures of offloading, separate assisted production from unaided comprehension, and show that apparent AI accuracy can rise through user adaptation even when the prediction policy is fixed. Evidence on distributional effects also develops the proposition: one Argentine experiment reports gains for both education groups but larger gains for less-educated participants, while persistent differences in effective use prevent full equalization. Material internal variation concerns evidential maturity and direction. Some sources report measured benefits, costs or heterogeneous effects, whereas many supplied excerpts provide only experimental designs and therefore cannot establish productivity outcomes. The legal sources are chiefly methodological, leaving professional legal-work effects particularly underdetermined. METR adds a further qualification: spreading adoption can select enthusiastic users and AI-suited tasks out of randomized comparisons, potentially biasing estimates downward, although omitted-task preferences do not prove actual gains. Overall, the period strengthens the cluster’s practical, local-evaluation framework rather than supporting a universal positive or negative productivity effect.
